routes.description: Establish that Jesus personally claimed divine identity by reading his titles, sayings, prerogatives, and reception cumulatively within a first-century Jewish two-powers framework and by defending that interpretation against delegated-authority alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant Jewish framework can include distinguishable divine figures, Jesus applies that identity framework to himself through words and functions, and the cumulative evidence is not adequately explained by mere agency, exalted humanity, or later attribution.

motionBridge.description: Connect Jesus's own claimed titles, authority, and functions to personal participation in divine identity rather than merely to later beliefs about him.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish scripture supplied a recognizable framework of distinguishable figures sharing Yahweh's identity and that Jesus located himself within it.
Show that Jesus's Son, Lord, Son of Man, divine-name, unity, and preexistence language communicates more than messianic or representative status.
Show that Jesus's claims to equal honor, universal judgment, life-giving authority, resurrection power, and premundane glory identify him with divine functions.
Connect followers' devotion and opponents' accusations to Jesus's self-claims while establishing that the resulting high christology is early rather than a late development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how receiving authority, serving, and distinguishing himself from the Father can coexist with prior divine identity through incarnation and exaltation.
Establish when worship language and hostile reactions reliably corroborate the intended force of Jesus's claims.

routes.description: Defeat the claim that Jesus personally identified himself as God by showing that the cited language, functions, and honors remain explicable through divine name-bearing, delegated agency, messianic or ideal-human status, and later high christology.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative cannot bridge from disputed texts and received authority to Jesus's own divine identity because viable agency readings remain, contrary dependence language persists, or early Christian portrayals do not establish Jesus's historical self-claim.

motionBridge.description: Show that exalted status, divine authorization, name-bearing, or later portrayal does not by itself establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish representatives could bear God's name, exercise transmitted authority, and receive deference without being identical with Yahweh.
Show that unity, glory, judgment, forgiveness, miraculous power, and other assertedly divine features are received by Jesus or extended to disciples.
Provide non-divine readings of the principal Johannine, Synoptic, Danielic, and Pauline terms and passages used to infer divine identity.
Separate claims made by Jesus from followers' devotion, authorial framing, later high christology, and historically disputed interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that blasphemy accusations, stoning attempts, and other reactions may reflect misunderstanding or charges that do not require a divine-identity claim.
Distinguish homage language applicable to non-divine recipients from cultic service that would uniquely identify its recipient as God.

sections.title: Two powers, divine name-bearing, and Jewish agency
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the controlling historical framework for deciding whether distinguishable Yahweh figures and divine name-bearing imply shared divine identity or delegated representation.

sections.title: Jesus's sayings, titles, and scriptural allusions
sections.rationale: The motion centrally depends on whether Son, Lord, Son of Man, unity, preexistence, and divine-name language constitutes Jesus's personal divine claim or permits non-divine readings.

sections.title: Divine prerogatives, dependence, and delegated authority
sections.rationale: Claims involving judgment, resurrection, life, forgiveness, glory, and Sabbath authority must be tested against language of receipt, dependence, prayer, and comparable grants to disciples.

sections.title: Worship, early devotion, and hostile reactions
sections.rationale: Followers' prayers and homage and opponents' blasphemy reactions may corroborate Jesus's intended claim, but their semantic force and reliability require independent assessment.

sections.title: Historical self-claim and christological development
sections.rationale: The debate requires separating Jesus's own claims from Gospel framing and early Christian christology while assessing Synoptic and Johannine differences, Pauline material, and proposed development.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Old Testament portrayals of two distinguishishable figures acting as Yahweh establish a two-powers framework within which Jesus identifies himself as one divine power.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening continues in Wood's voice and develops the two-powers thesis announced immediately beforehand.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative's controlling Jewish scriptural framework and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central route premise through several announced scriptural examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-powers thesis is recoverable, but the move compresses the distinction between two divine figures and two persons sharing divine identity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited scriptural pattern strongly supports distinguishable heavenly figures, though its application to shared identity requires an implicit further bridge.

charity.alternative: The angel or second figure may be an authorized representative rather than a distinct participant in Yahweh's identity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinction and divine speech alone do not determine whether the figure possesses identity or delegated agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples form a coherent pattern, but the inference from distinguishable Yahweh figures to Jesus occupying a divine power leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Old Testament examples and a named historical framework support the thesis, with the representative-agency rival insufficiently compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the historical framework on which much of the affirmative route depends.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges historical ways of handling the passages but does not fully compare the strongest agency interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly asserts monotheism alongside numerous Old Testament passages containing two divine figures and announces concrete examples.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus presents himself as the unique Son, David's heavenly Lord, and Daniel's cloud-riding Son of Man, thereby claiming the identity of a heavenly divine power.
moves.attributionBasis: This extended textual argument remains within Wood's uninterrupted affirmative opening and uses his announced category of what Jesus says.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the motion by connecting Jesus's attributed titles and trial language to his own claimed heavenly identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely supplies self-claim evidence through linked titles and a specific Danielic allusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The asserted title-based inference is clear and stable, although the qualification that heavenly status need not entail Yahweh identity remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Danielic cloud-rider and right-hand language provide substantial support, but the move states the divine-identity conclusion more strongly than the compressed warrant alone establishes.

charity.alternative: The Son of Man may be an exalted messianic or representative figure who receives authority from God without sharing God's identity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Daniel 7 distinguishes the figure from the Ancient of Days and depicts authority being given to him.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The linked titles and scriptural allusion support a coherent cumulative inference, with one bounded but important identity bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move uses specific sayings and Daniel 7 imagery, though it does not seriously compare exalted-messianic and delegated-authority readings.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is near the top of motion-tier relevance because it directly concerns what Jesus personally claims at his trial.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move emphasizes divine cloud imagery but does not adequately address the strongest received-authority reading of the same passage.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected evidence identifies Jesus with Daniel's cloud-coming Son of Man seated beside the divine power and explicitly draws the self-claim inference.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus claims divine status by assuming Yahweh's roles as universal judge and raiser of the dead while requiring honor equal to the Father's.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood remains the sole speaker and explicitly transitions from what Jesus says to what Jesus does in support of his affirmative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies direct motion evidence by joining Jesus's attributed functions and demanded honor to a personal claim of divine status.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it closely connects a specific saying and asserted divine functions to the motion's decisive identity bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The central proposition is clear, but the move shifts between exclusive divine functions and functions expressly given to the Son without fully delimiting scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Equal honor and eschatological functions are substantial evidence, while the text's grant language creates a material qualification not made explicit.

charity.alternative: The Father may grant judicial and life-giving authority to an exalted agent without making that agent identical with God.
charity.decisiveQualification: John 5 expressly says judgment is given or entrusted to the Son even while requiring equal honor.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from equal honor and Yahweh-associated functions is plausible, but exclusivity and granted authority require a material explanatory bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: John 5 provides specific textual support, but the warrant from entrusted functions to personal divine identity remains incompletely defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within motion contact, the move directly attempts to establish Jesus's personal divine status from his own attributed words and roles.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move quotes the grant language but does not meaningfully explain it before treating the functions as identifying Jesus with God.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes John 5 on all judgment being given to the Son, equal honor for Father and Son, and Jesus raising the dead.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: The earliest Christians treated Jesus as divine Lord and creative Word, applied Yahweh's name and honors to him, and directed worship, prayer, hymns, baptism, and liturgy toward him.
moves.attributionBasis: The material completes Wood's opening before the moderator explicitly announces the end of David Wood's statement and Alex's turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move supports the early-corroboration bridge through the practices and descriptions attributed to the earliest Christian community.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it offers a broad and concrete devotion pattern, though its connection to Jesus's own self-claim is indirect.

precisionFindings.rationale: The list of devotional practices is clear, but the breadth of 'earliest Christians' and the cultic force of every listed practice are compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cumulative practices support very high christology, but they do not without qualification establish Jesus's historical personal claim.

charity.alternative: Early followers could direct exalted devotion toward Jesus without thereby preserving a personal claim Jesus historically made about himself.
charity.decisiveQualification: Follower practice establishes their christology directly but Jesus's self-understanding only indirectly.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The devotional evidence coherently supports early high christology, but its use as evidence of Jesus's own claim needs an additional historical bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific practices provide representative support, while dating, semantic force, and independence from later portrayal remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it strongly advances cumulative corroboration but bears on the personal-claim motion only indirectly.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move forcefully catalogs devotion but gives insufficient attention to the decisive distinction between reception and historical self-claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt enumerates worship, prayer, hymns, baptism, liturgy, and doxologies directed toward Jesus as a full array of religious honors.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus's appeal to Psalm 82 answers the charge of claiming deity by comparing his title with non-Yahweh beings called gods and by identifying himself as God's consecrated and sent Son.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator transfers the podium to Alex, whose opening then explicitly addresses David's two-powers interpretation and develops this counterreading.

components.text: Whether Jesus's own title and scriptural usage identifies him as a divine heavenly power rather than an authorized Son.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive self-claim inference by offering Jesus's Psalm 82 appeal as an express non-Yahweh explanation of divine terminology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly challenges the identity inference with Jesus's stated comparison and sent-Son description.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed reading, comparison class, and consequence for the blasphemy charge are all stated clearly and with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a definite contextual reading while grounding it in the cited comparison to non-Yahweh beings called gods.

charity.alternative: Jesus may use an a-fortiori defense that does not retract the stronger divine implication of his unique consecration and sonship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Psalm 82 can answer an accusation pragmatically without exhausting John's larger characterization of Jesus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparison to other beings called gods and Jesus's sent-Son description yield a clear alternative inference without internal tension.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move uses the immediate Psalm 82 context specifically, though the larger Johannine context and a-fortiori rival remain bounded gaps.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supports the motion-level failure bridge by contesting that Jesus's own words amount to a claim of deity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents the affirmative motivation fairly but somewhat compresses the possibility that the defense is strategic rather than reductive.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly reasons from Psalm 82's non-Yahweh gods to Jesus's consecrated and sent status as God's Son.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even if Jesus's 'I am' language evokes Exodus, Jewish traditions permit a non-Yahweh representative to bear God's name and exercise God's authority, so name-bearing does not establish identity with Yahweh.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor remains the uninterrupted speaker, introduces John 8 as another major christological claim, and carries the argument through the final delivered context row.

components.text: The inference that divine-name or Yahweh-associated language necessarily identifies Jesus personally with Yahweh.
Whether Jewish divine-figure traditions exclude representative name-bearing agency.

response.rationale: The reply identifies a failure in the identity inference: contemporary Jewish representatives could bear Yahweh's name and exercise his authority without being Yahweh.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly names the invalid necessity inference and supplies the defeating representative-agency consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The agency alternative and its limited consequence—that name-bearing alone is insufficient—are expressly and stably formulated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not deny an Exodus echo; it appropriately argues that such an echo underdetermines identity given the stated agency tradition.

charity.alternative: Jesus may bear the divine name in a uniquely identity-sharing manner exceeding ordinary representation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The existence of transferable name-bearing defeats necessity but does not independently prove that Jesus is merely an agent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample structure is explicit: if non-Yahweh agents can bear the name, name-bearing cannot by itself entail Yahweh identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a relevant Jewish tradition but the selected evidence does not document representative examples or their precise comparability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level bridge from Jesus's language to personal divine identity by supplying a viable agency explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the affirmative's Exodus imagery and confines its objection to the inference, with only a minor comparison gap about uniqueness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes an Exodus 3 echo and states that roughly contemporary Jewish texts endow non-Yahweh beings with Yahweh's name and representative authority.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: John 8:58 can present Jesus as the fulfillment eternally planned in Abraham's promised redemption rather than asserting Jesus's personal preexistence or identity with Yahweh.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation remains within O'Connor’s opening statement and develops his previously established critical interpretation.

components.text: Whether Johannine preexistence language requires Jesus's personal preexistence and divine identity.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the textual inference by proposing that Abraham's joy concerns an eternally planned redemption fulfilled in Jesus rather than Jesus's personal preexistence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive interpretive component but openly leaves the present-tense wording as a substantial difficulty.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is clearly labeled possible and expressly qualified by acknowledgment that the present-tense wording remains strange.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly presents the reading as a suggestion and directly acknowledges the textual feature that counts against it.

charity.alternative: The present-tense 'I am' states Jesus's actual preexistence before Abraham and may evoke the divine name.
charity.decisiveQualification: The unusual tense remains evidence against reducing the saying to promised fulfillment alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The promised-fulfillment reading is possible and internally coherent, but the relation between Abraham's promised day and 'I am' remains materially underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A common redemption tradition is invoked, but the crucial grammatical and contextual verification needed to prefer this reading is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it supplies a direct non-divine reading of a principal Johannine saying, though only as a possibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly voices the strongest preexistence difficulty and limits its own alternative to a cautious possibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Abraham's joy to promised redemption from the beginning while candidly noting the strange present-tense claim and apparent preexistence.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: An attempt to stone Jesus does not establish that his opponents correctly understood him as claiming deity, because Johannine opponents repeatedly misunderstand him and blasphemy accusations can arise from broader alleged offenses.
moves.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted opening statement explicitly examines the significance of blasphemy accusations and compares Jesus with Stephen.

components.text: Whether hostile reactions reliably corroborate the intended divine force of Jesus's disputed words.
Whether opponents' accusation establishes the correct meaning of Jesus's claim.

response.rationale: The reply identifies why hostile reaction is unreliable evidence: Johannine opponents recurrently misunderstand Jesus, and blasphemy charges need not specify divine identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly attacks the reaction-based warrant and states that stoning cannot settle the intended meaning.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely argues underdetermination rather than claiming that every hostile reaction is mistaken or wholly irrelevant.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The recurring misunderstanding motif appropriately warrants skepticism about treating hostile reaction as decisive interpretive evidence.

charity.alternative: A stoning attempt immediately following a saying can still provide contextual evidence about how the saying sounded to contemporary hearers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Misunderstanding makes that evidence defeasible, not necessarily worthless.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is explicit and valid: systematically misunderstanding opponents cannot independently guarantee the correctness of their divine-claim interpretation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Johannine misunderstanding motif and broader blasphemy category support the objection, with contextual reaction still retaining some evidential value.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly addresses whether hostile reactions reliably corroborate Jesus's intended claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The sarcastic presentation remains substantively fair because it identifies the affirmative use before limiting rather than eliminating reaction evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt highlights the Gospel theme that Jesus's opponents repeatedly misunderstand him and rejects their reaction as automatically sound exegesis.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Scriptural interaction between Yahweh and the angel of Yahweh supports two distinguishable heavenly powers rather than reducing the angel to a merely delegated human representative.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Wood’s rebuttal, after which Wood explicitly summarizes his opening and answers O'Connor’s delegated-authority proposal.

components.text: Whether the relevant Yahweh figure is adequately explained as a merely delegated representative.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the agency alternative through Genesis 22's interaction and speaker alternation, arguing for distinguishable heavenly powers rather than ordinary representation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly supplies a counterexample pattern, though it does not fully distinguish divine agency from shared identity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scriptural distinction is clear, but 'power' and the boundary between divine manifestation, agency, and person remain partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interaction supports distinction and unusual identification, but it does not alone exclude a robust angelic-agency account.

charity.alternative: The angel can speak and act with Yahweh's authority as a principal agent while remaining ontologically distinct from Yahweh.
charity.decisiveQualification: First-person divine speech and interaction require explanation but are compatible with some ancient agency conventions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The textual interaction coherently challenges reduction to a human representative, but the step from heavenly distinction to shared divine identity remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genesis 22 supplies specific evidence, while the competing agency convention and representative comparanda are not seriously evaluated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the reply directly attacks the name-bearing-agency bridge using the controlling scriptural framework.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets a merely human representative but does not fully confront the stronger heavenly-agent version of the objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt develops Genesis 22's alternating references to God and the angel of the Lord as evidence of distinguishable heavenly speakers.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Stephen's vision and prayer to Jesus, together with the earliest Christians calling on Jesus's name, show Jesus receiving Yahweh-associated devotion within roughly two years of the crucifixion.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood explicitly turns to O'Connor’s Stephen example and sustains the rebuttal through Stephen’s prayer and the earliest Christian invocation of Jesus.

components.text: Whether Stephen's death and invocation show only a broader blasphemy offense rather than divine devotion to Jesus.
Whether calling on Jesus's name is adequately explained as representative name-bearing.

response.rationale: The reply supplies Stephen's prayer and very early invocation of Jesus as evidence that Jesus received Yahweh-associated devotion, contacting both historical and agency objections.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it presents directly contrary devotional evidence, though it does not fully resolve the historical self-claim distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The devotion claim is clear, but the dating to roughly two years and the scope of earliest Christian practice carry implicit qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Prayer to Jesus strongly supports early high devotion, while exact dating and its inference to Jesus's own claim are stated too firmly.

charity.alternative: Stephen's and early Christians' invocation establishes their high view of Jesus but not necessarily Jesus's historical self-understanding.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early reception narrows a late-development explanation without directly supplying a saying by Jesus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidence coherently establishes early devotion, but the further inference from early follower practice to Jesus's personal claim remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Stephen's prayer and Paul's early conversion provide specific chronological support, with exact dating and historical transmission insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it strongly addresses early corroboration and self-claim separation, though its evidence remains indirect.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move effectively addresses lateness but insufficiently preserves the decisive distinction between follower devotion and personal self-claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that Christians called on Jesus as they should call on Yahweh and dates this practice near Paul's conversion shortly after the crucifixion.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus receives and then delegates glory, judgment, and forgiveness, showing that possession of these allegedly divine prerogatives can reflect transmitted authority rather than personal identity as God.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor continues his rebuttal, explicitly answers Wood’s John 17 argument, and extends the same delegation principle to judgment and forgiveness.

components.text: Whether judgment, forgiveness, and glory uniquely identify their possessor as God.
Whether honors or prerogatives directed to Jesus necessarily establish divine identity.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the exclusivity warrant as failing because Jesus receives and delegates comparable prerogatives to disciples, defeating the inference from possession alone.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly identifies the inference, supplies several counterexamples, and states their defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently limits its conclusion to the non-exclusivity and transferability of the cited prerogatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The textual grants provide a strong warrant that possession of these functions alone cannot entail personal identity as God.

charity.alternative: Jesus may possess these prerogatives universally or intrinsically while disciples exercise only limited derivative forms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Differences in scope and mode of possession can preserve evidential force even when a function is transferable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample reasoning is explicit and valid against a bare exclusivity premise, subject to a bounded difference-of-scope qualification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Judgment over tribes and delegated forgiveness are specific textual examples, though equivalence with Jesus's universal roles is not fully established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supports motion-level failure by attacking a principal inference from divine prerogatives to Jesus's personal identity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes delegation but presses rhetorical parity more strongly than the potentially decisive scope differences warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Jesus granting judgment to disciples and forgiveness authority in John, using these examples against the claim that such functions are God-exclusive.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The Gospels' pervasive misunderstanding and the Synoptic messianic-secret motif make it difficult to treat the record as evidence that Jesus clearly and publicly communicated a personal claim to be God.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person rebuttal follows Alex's identified speaking turn and directly addresses David's communication argument.

components.text: Whether the Gospel record shows Jesus clearly communicating the proposed personal divine claim to his hearers.
Whether early follower understanding establishes what Jesus himself clearly disclosed.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the communication and historical-self-claim issue by contrasting alleged public divine claims with pervasive misunderstanding and the Synoptic secrecy motif.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it squarely identifies a tension in the affirmative account, although obscurity alone does not determine semantic content.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move argues that the evidence creates difficulty for clear public disclosure, not that obscurity logically disproves every divine claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated motifs warrant a substantial historical tension, and the move appropriately frames the conclusion as difficulty rather than impossibility.

charity.alternative: Jesus may intentionally reveal identity progressively or in veiled scriptural allusions, explaining misunderstanding and secrecy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect disclosure can be genuine, but it weakens claims that any competent contemporary hearer would clearly understand it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The tension between allegedly obvious public claims and pervasive secrecy is well formed, though it challenges clarity more directly than truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Synoptic secret and misunderstanding motifs are concrete evidence, while Gospel-specific variation and narrative purposes remain undercompared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it materially supports separating Gospel interpretation and follower reception from Jesus's historical self-claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages the public-clarity version fairly, with a minor omission concerning progressive narrative disclosure.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts supposedly unmistakable divine-name claims with the Synoptic motif in which Jesus restricts disclosure of his identity.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus's acceptance of proskynesis does not establish deity because the term can denote bodily homage to human authorities, whereas the New Testament uses distinct language for cultic service reserved for God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly pivots to worship terminology and sustains a lexical and comparative scriptural argument until the rebuttal closes.

components.text: Whether proskynesis directed to Jesus is worship whose recipient must be God.
Whether every form of devotion mentioned has uniquely cultic semantic force.

response.rationale: The reply directly defeats the lexical inference from proskynesis by citing human recipients, but it does not answer the distinct evidence from prayer and invocation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive proskynesis component but leaves the broader array of devotional practices unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully distinguishes bodily homage from uniquely cultic service and does not claim that all worship vocabulary is interchangeable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Human recipients of the same term strongly warrant the limited conclusion that proskynesis alone does not establish deity.

charity.alternative: Context can elevate a normally flexible homage term into divine worship when combined with other cultic practices and christological framing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lexical non-exclusivity defeats a word-level entailment but not a contextual cumulative argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The human-recipient counterexamples decisively refute the claim that the term itself can apply only to God.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The parable and Revelation provide specific comparative usages, though the separate cultic-service terminology is only briefly defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly supports the worship-semantics bridge while leaving other devotional evidence intact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly limits the lexical claim and supplies counterexamples, with only a minor omission about cumulative contextual force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites proskynesis offered to a human master and promised before human followers in Revelation as direct lexical counterexamples.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Philippians 2 depicts a preexistent divine being who voluntarily assumes human likeness and receives universal homage, rather than an ordinary image-bearing human elevated only afterward.
moves.attributionBasis: David identifies Alex's use of a scholarly reading, quotes and interprets the hymn's sequence, and concludes with its application of Isaiah's Yahweh language.

components.text: Whether early non-Johannine material contains a divine-incarnation conception despite Synoptic obscurity.
Whether exaltation and received homage imply only an ordinary human elevated afterward.

response.rationale: The reply contacts development and delegation objections by interpreting Philippians' sequence as preexistent voluntary incarnation followed by exaltation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly engages the rival human-exaltation reading through the grammatical and narrative sequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The preexistence-versus-human-exaltation contrast and the claimed temporal sequence are stated clearly and consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The sequence of self-emptying before human likeness provides substantial warrant, although competing Adamic interpretations remain possible.

charity.alternative: Philippians 2 may portray an Adamic human refusing grasping and then receiving exaltation rather than a preexistent divine person incarnating.
charity.decisiveQualification: The ordering of self-humbling, servant form, and human likeness is the central disputed interpretive feature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The temporal-sequence inference is explicit and coherent, with the main remaining issue being interpretation rather than validity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quoted sequence specifically supports preexistence, while broader hymn context and the strongest Adamic scholarly warrant remain only partly compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it strongly attacks later-development and mere-human readings, though Paul remains indirect evidence of Jesus's self-claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately states and directly contests the human reading, though its informal caricature slightly understates that reading's exegetical basis.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes that the decision to humble himself precedes being made in human likeness and explicitly contrasts an ordinary Adamic human reading.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus's use of the Septuagint's doubled Kyrios formula points to Yahweh and, alongside the shared conclusions of followers and enemies, supports an intentionally veiled but genuine divine claim.
moves.attributionBasis: David moves from the Greek formula into a connected response about careful communication and the concordant reactions attributed to Jesus's friends and enemies.

components.text: Whether veiled communication and misunderstanding are compatible with a genuine scripturally encoded divine claim.
Whether the Septuagint's doubled Kyrios formula specifically identifies the referent with Yahweh.

response.rationale: The reply contacts obscurity and name-bearing objections by arguing that Jesus used a specifically Yahwistic Septuagint formula while communicating carefully rather than plainly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it offers a direct textual answer, though the claimed formula's exclusivity and exact citation remain underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended inference is recoverable, but the doubled formula, its alleged exclusivity, and the separate friends-and-enemies corroboration are compressed together.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The selected evidence asserts that the formula specifically and uniquely refers to Yahweh without enough linguistic or contextual demonstration.

charity.alternative: A Septuagintal Kyrios formula may quote Yahweh-language while still being applied through messianic agency or authorial framing.
